Scene Representation in Unreal Engine

Follow one indoor room from shared geometry and placed components through animation, GPU records, visible surfaces, and lighting representations—with real Unreal captures.

Scene representation ↑

A triangle is enough to begin a renderer. Give the GPU three positions, tell it where the camera is, and ask it to color the pixels inside their projected outline. A game engine becomes difficult when that triangle belongs to a reusable object, the object moves while the previous frame is still rendering, a thousand copies share its geometry, and a shadow or reflection needs to see it from somewhere other than the player's camera. Scene representation is the machinery that keeps all of those descriptions coherent.

We will follow one indoor room from an editable level to the pixels of an image. The room is four meters wide, five meters deep, and three meters high, open toward the camera. Its red and green side walls, pale floor and ceiling, matte block, glossy block, and ceiling area light give us recognizable objects to follow through every representation. The image below is an actual capture of Unreal 5.8.1. Later buffer views and lighting diagnostics use this same geometry and camera.

The room grows only when a new question needs another object. First we isolate a small floor patch to understand vertices, indices, transforms, and materials. Then we add an indoor door with an attached indicator, a skeletal mannequin, and three potted plants to expose attachment, deformation, and instancing. Finally, optional fixtures—a cable, a heightfield exhibit, an editable wall panel, a basin, smoke, and a scan of this room—test geometry contracts that ordinary cubes cannot exercise. We return to the seven-piece baseline for controlled material and lighting comparisons.

Keep three evidence labels in mind. Baseline capture means the original seven-component room rendered by Unreal. Extension capture means that room with the door, mannequin, and plants actually added; its inventory records the changes. Worked example means a computed close-up or a proposed fixture in this room. For example, the four-vertex floor patch below explains indexing; it is not a claim that Unreal's built-in cube has only four render vertices. Likewise, the later smoke and groom diagrams specify extensions, not features secretly present in the baseline screenshot.

The Unreal names arrive after the problem that makes them useful: an asset when geometry must be shared, a component when an object is placed, a render proxy when threads need independent access, and GPU Scene when shaders must address many placements. We will carry the same object identities through those boundaries. The final Arda design is a proposal derived from these obligations, not a description of existing Arda scene classes.

01A triangle becomes an object

Isolate a one-meter square patch of the room’s floor as a teaching tile. Imagine that tile lying in its own local coordinate system. Its four corners are (0,0,0), (100,0,0), (100,100,0), and (0,100,0), in Unreal's usual centimeter units. Four positions do not yet say which regions form a surface. We also need connectivity. An index array [0,1,2, 0,2,3] says that the first triangle uses corners zero, one, and two, while the second uses zero, two, and three. The two triangles share two corners. This is an indexed triangle mesh: a vertex array supplies attributes, and an index array chooses which vertex records each triangle uses.

A vertex record usually contains more than position. A surface normal describes an orientation for shading. A tangent supplies a direction along the surface, useful when interpreting a normal map. Texture coordinates, conventionally called UV coordinates, give a two-dimensional address into a texture: (0,0) might mean its lower left corner and (1,1) its upper right, subject to sampling conventions. Colors and other attributes can also be stored per vertex. At a texture seam, two vertices may have the same position but different UVs. They must be separate render vertices even though a modeling tool may present them as one geometric corner.

This distinction already explains why an imported model and a GPU buffer are different representations. A modeler may work with polygons, smoothing groups, named surfaces, and convenient shared control points. Rendering needs triangles, the exact attribute combinations at their corners, and compact buffers with a known layout. The engine's asset-building process performs this conversion and may produce several levels of detail. An LOD is a version appropriate to a particular viewing scale; it is not a separate object in the world. The tile can refer to the same asset while the renderer chooses a less detailed version when it occupies fewer pixels.

Unreal's conventional static-mesh representation makes these distinctions concrete. FStaticMeshLODResources owns the render resources for one LOD, including vertex buffers, an index buffer, and sections. A section describes a range of triangles that share a material slot and related rendering flags. FStaticMeshVertexBuffers groups position, general static-mesh vertex attributes, and color buffers. None of these structures says where a particular tile lies in our room. They describe reusable geometry. The relevant declarations are in StaticMeshResources.h.

The tables throughout this article select the information needed to follow the scene. A named field is real Unreal data; a named operation describes information an interface provides. Neither implies that the complete C++ object is uploaded to the GPU. Read each row as a connection between a piece of information and the problem it solves.

Now place a floor tile inside the room. Its local lower corner is (0,0,0); translate it by (−50,200,0) cm. Local corner (100,0,0) becomes world corner (50,200,0). The tile occupies a small square of the floor, from X = −50 to 50 and Y = 200 to 300. These are numerical exercise coordinates in the room, not the centered local coordinates of the captured cube asset. For the next projection diagram only, an overhead teaching camera sits at (−100,200,400) and looks along −Z. The ordinary room screenshots retain their original camera near the open front. Changing the observation never rewrites the tile’s shared local vertices.

It is tempting to call each copy a mesh, but that word would now hide two different costs. The asset consumes geometry storage and streaming bandwidth. Each placement consumes an identity, a transform, bounds, and whatever parameters distinguish its appearance. A thousand tiles should not require a thousand copies of their vertex arrays. They still require a thousand placements, because the engine must cull them, address them, and potentially move or remove one independently. GPU instancing reduces repeated submission work by drawing compatible placements together; it does not eliminate the underlying distinction.

The first material on our tile can be equally simple: a constant pale color and a roughness value. Roughness controls how broadly the surface reflects a light. Geometry alone cannot provide those values, and a transform cannot provide them either. Our smallest useful scene description therefore has three independent references: geometry, placement, and appearance. A camera supplies a fourth input, because a picture depends on where the scene is observed. A light supplies a fifth, because the surface's response and the illumination reaching it are different facts. These distinctions are conceptually useful even in a renderer consisting of a few hundred lines.

One more piece of data becomes necessary before we can afford a thousand tiles: bounds. A bounding box or sphere encloses the geometry in a form that is cheap to test. If a tile's bounds are outside the camera's view volume, the renderer can skip detailed work. Bounds are a promise that all relevant geometry lies inside. They are deliberately simpler than the mesh. When later chapters introduce animation and displacement, remember that changing the shape can invalidate this promise even when the object origin has not moved.

02The world is not one tree

We now need to let a level designer place the room’s objects and attach a small indicator to its indoor door. Unreal organizes gameplay objects with actors and components. An AActor is an object that can belong to a world and participate in gameplay. Components divide its behavior into reusable pieces. A component might render a mesh, play audio, or implement some other service; the word component does not imply visible geometry. Unreal's UObject infrastructure provides reflected types, serialization, editor integration, and managed object references. These are valuable authoring facilities, but they do not prescribe how a GPU should read a million placements.

The component inheritance chain adds responsibilities incrementally. UActorComponent supplies the basic component lifecycle. USceneComponent adds a transform and attachment relationships. UPrimitiveComponent adds the contract for a renderable or collision-bearing primitive, including bounds and scene integration. Here a render primitive means an object registered with the rendering scene; it does not mean one triangle. One such object can contain thousands of triangles or many placements of a shared mesh. A collision-only component can also exist without producing a visible render proxy. UMeshComponent supplies mesh-related facilities such as materials, and UStaticMeshComponent is a concrete component that can refer to a UStaticMesh asset. This is a class hierarchy: it explains which behavior an implementation inherits. It does not say which object is attached to which other object in our room. The inheritance is visible directly in SceneComponent.h, PrimitiveComponent.h, and MeshComponent.h.

For the indoor door, imagine an actor containing a root scene component at its hinge, a door mesh and a small indicator both attached to that root. The extension capture builds this relationship explicitly. Turning the hinge changes both world transforms, while their relative offsets remain meaningful. The door and indicator use separate mesh components; the indicator is an emissive marker with no separate light component in the captured scene. An optional PointLightComponent could attach to the same hierarchy without becoming part of either mesh. Actor ownership, component attachment, and asset sharing are different relationships even when an editor presents them near each other.

An actor's root component provides its principal transform. In the source, AActor::RootComponent is a USceneComponent reference, and retrieving the actor transform delegates to that component when it exists. This matters when designing an equivalent system: a useful gameplay container does not need to be the universal node that owns all transform arithmetic. Unreal can express a transform-only attachment node with no mesh, a mesh-bearing node, and several visible components owned by one actor. Actor.h exposes that distinction plainly.

The renderer needs another organization. To decide what is visible, it needs spatial bounds, visibility flags, and efficient arrays or spatial structures. The floor and matte block have no attachment relationship, yet both use the cube asset and can participate in similar rendering work. Conversely, the door and its attached indicator share motion ancestry while requiring their own material bindings. A visibility hierarchy groups objects because of space. A draw grouping groups them because of compatible rendering state. Neither should be forced to mirror the attachment hierarchy.

This is the first major architectural lesson. A scene is not adequately described by one recursive tree whose nodes own everything. It is a collection of related records with different lifetimes and access patterns. The authoring model may be a convenient tree, while the rendering model is a set of dense arrays. Our mannequin adds a bone hierarchy inside one renderable object. A mesh asset adds an LOD hierarchy. Nanite adds a hierarchy of geometry clusters. None is a replacement for the others, because each hierarchy answers a different question.

Unreal makes the renderer's separate organization explicit in FScene. Its packed arrays include primitive pointers, transforms, bounds, flags, and component IDs. The comments explain that a primitive's packed index addresses corresponding entries across these arrays. This is a practical structure-of-arrays pattern: a visibility pass can inspect bounds and flags without walking every gameplay object or loading every material. A different stage can follow a primitive reference to richer rendering information. The layout is described in ScenePrivate.h.

For Arda, the consequence is immediate even before choosing an entity system. Preserve attachment relationships where they are useful for authoring and transform propagation. Resolve the resulting world transforms into a renderer-facing representation. Preserve geometry sharing with explicit asset handles. Let culling, sorting, and GPU allocation organize their own data. Modularity comes from keeping these meanings separate, then defining how a change in one representation updates the others. It does not come from giving every possible object the same enormous base class.

03Crossing the thread boundary

The door begins to swing while the GPU is drawing the previous frame. Which transform should the renderer read? If it directly follows the gameplay component's mutable fields, it can observe a mixture of times: the new transform, the old bounds, and a material reference being replaced. Locking every access could restore consistency, but it would also couple rendering progress to gameplay progress. The problem is not merely that threads are dangerous. The two systems need permission to advance independently while agreeing on complete versions of scene state.

Unreal's basic answer is a render proxy. FPrimitiveSceneProxy holds the rendering-facing state of a primitive and provides specialized behavior for that primitive type. The source describes it as mirrored data for rendering a UPrimitiveComponent in parallel with the game thread, and explicitly expects subclasses for different primitive types. A static mesh supplies one implementation; a skeletal mesh or a landscape supplies another. The proxy is a bridge from an authoring object into renderer-owned behavior, not an instruction to serialize an entire actor hierarchy into a second copy. See the contract in PrimitiveSceneProxy.h.

For the door, the proxy is the renderer-facing description of how this kind of primitive can be drawn. It combines copied state with virtual operations; geometry buffers and material choices often belong to its concrete subclass or referenced resources. The following table describes the base contract, not a promise that every subtype supports every path.

The debugging component pointer in this class is explicitly unsuitable for render-thread reads of gameplay state. Copying the transform into a proxy solves a concurrency problem; retaining a pointer to the original component does not remove that problem.

When the tile component creates its render state, UPrimitiveComponent::CreateRenderState_Concurrent updates bounds and, if it should be in the scene, adds the primitive through a registration context or through GetWorld()->Scene. The latter is an FSceneInterface, which exposes scene operations without making every engine component depend on the private renderer implementation. A component knows it can add or update a primitive; it does not need to know how the deferred renderer stores its internal arrays. The call is visible in PrimitiveComponent.cpp.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: SceneInterface.h.

The renderer-side scene integration introduces FPrimitiveSceneInfo. Keep its role distinct from the proxy. The proxy describes the primitive's rendering behavior and mirrored properties. The scene info manages the primitive's membership in a particular FScene: indices, cached drawing information, links to lighting and other scene systems, and lifecycle state. This split allows a geometry implementation to provide its meshes while the renderer manages where those meshes fit into the current scene. The declaration of FPrimitiveSceneInfo and its scene-management methods is in PrimitiveSceneInfo.h.

There is one scene-info record for the registered primitive proxy. Its data answers where the primitive is registered and which renderer records already exist for it. Optional lighting, Nanite and ray-tracing entries below are populated according to the primitive and enabled path.

If only the hinge transform changes, the scene updates copied placement, bounds and affected derived data. If the geometry description changes, cached meshes or commands may need rebuilding. If the door disappears, its scene membership and allocations must be retired. The proxy describes what the producer can render; scene info tracks how that producer currently participates in this scene.

The source directories reinforce this boundary. The Engine module contains the component and primitive-proxy contracts, while the Renderer module supplies FScene and renderer-specific scene information. RenderCore provides common rendering machinery such as shader and vertex-factory infrastructure. RHI, the rendering hardware interface, expresses buffers, textures, and commands for backend implementations. These are dependency boundaries rather than a requirement that every call move one step down a class tree. A component submits a semantic scene change; a pass eventually records hardware-facing work. Keeping the interface at the shared dependency boundary allows specialized producers to participate without exposing the renderer's entire private implementation.

The add path illustrates the handoff precisely. Unreal creates a primitive scene info, associates it with the proxy, captures the render matrix and bounds, and collects an add command. It then enqueues rendering work that sets the proxy transform, creates its render-thread resources, and attaches the scene info. Capturing those values makes the handoff deliberate. The render-side work consumes a prepared description; it does not need to rediscover the transform by traversing mutable actor state later. The ordering is explicit in RendererScene.cpp.

This is also why a pointer back to a component is not an invitation to read it from the render thread. FPrimitiveSceneInfo retains a debugging-only component interface pointer, but its comment explicitly warns against dereferencing it on the rendering thread because gameplay may modify the object concurrently. Identity may cross the boundary without granting read access to mutable state. In a custom engine, a stable handle plus a copied snapshot is often a clearer contract than a convenient raw pointer. Unreal's warning is in PrimitiveSceneInfo.h.

A camera introduces another lifetime. A render scene can persist for thousands of frames, but the current view describes a particular observation: matrices, viewport, show flags, and other view-dependent settings. Unreal uses FSceneView and related view-family structures for this purpose, with renderer-specific extensions for working state. The tile belongs to the persistent scene. Whether it is visible in the player's camera, a reflection capture, or a shadow view is a question asked of that scene. Storing a single global “visible” bit on the tile would confuse those observations.

The thread boundary therefore has two effects. It protects ownership, and it forces the engine to name what rendering actually needs. The proxy is not the gameplay object with fewer methods. It is a representation selected for a different consumer. An expandable system benefits from making that selection explicit: which fields are copied, which resources are shared with stable lifetime, which updates can be incremental, and which operations must recreate the representation. These questions become more consequential when the scene is also consumed by GPU culling and ray tracing.

04Check the asset and component boundary against the room

Return to the baseline introduced at the start and inspect its actual object records. The room was constructed and rendered in the local Unreal 5.8.1 editor on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell using DX12 and Shader Model 6. Its seven visible cube components provide a measured version of the sharing and registration contracts we have just derived. They are the same baseline used in the independent Lumen essay; the additional fixtures later in this article are kept in a separate extension map so these controlled comparisons stay reproducible.

In the baseline, seven visible static-mesh components make the room: five enclosing surfaces and two blocks. All seven refer to /Engine/BasicShapes/Cube.Cube. There are seven placements and one shared mesh asset, with five material assets. The floor, ceiling and back wall share the neutral material. This is an unusually useful example because the relationship is measurable: duplicating a box-shaped object does not require duplicating the cube's vertex buffer. Each component supplies its own placement and material binding.

The authoring script creates a StaticMeshActor, obtains its StaticMeshComponent, calls set_static_mesh with the shared cube, assigns a material, and sets the actor's scale and location. Those are public authoring operations. When the component registers, the render-state lifecycle described in the previous chapter creates the rendering representation. The script does not directly allocate an FPrimitiveSceneInfo, write GPU Scene buffers, or create draw commands. Those are consequences of registration and renderer processing.

The bound is attained at a box corner for each axis, so it is the exact AABB of the transformed box. It is still only a bound on the mesh. This distinction becomes critical for rotated thin objects and for deformation that extends beyond the asset's original box.

05Changes have lifetimes

Suppose the hinge rotates by five degrees. Rebuilding the door's vertex buffers would be wasteful because its local shape has not changed. Rebuilding the entire render proxy may also be unnecessary. The minimal change is a new world transform and corresponding bounds, together with any history needed to describe motion. Unreal exposes a transform-update path separately from render-state recreation. UPrimitiveComponent::SendRenderTransform_Concurrent updates bounds and calls UpdatePrimitiveTransform on the scene when the primitive is relevant to rendering. PrimitiveComponent.cpp is a useful example of representing a semantic change rather than declaring everything dirty.

Now replace the tile's material with glass. This may change which passes can draw it, whether it writes depth, and which shaders or draw commands are valid. Treating that as a new scalar in the transform table would miss its consequences. Conversely, changing a tint parameter inside a compatible material instance may leave the geometry and pass structure intact. Changing the mesh's triangle indices affects another category of state, potentially including acceleration structures used by ray tracing. A robust update system distinguishes these cases because their dependent work differs.

Unreal's component lifecycle maintains dirty states and deferred render updates. MarkRenderStateDirty records the need for render-state recreation, while the component update path also handles transform and dynamic-data changes. The renderer collects scene changes and applies them in its scene-update machinery. FScene::UpdateAllPrimitiveSceneInfos is a major coordination point for that work; its implementation includes material-uniform updates and the subsequent scene maintenance. These are not instructions to copy the entire scene every frame. They are facilities for collecting changes and updating the structures that depend on them. See ActorComponent.cpp and RendererScene.cpp.

Batching matters even when each individual update is small. Consider a stress-test variant of the planter display containing two hundred leaf instances on a moving tray. Gameplay may propagate two hundred new transforms. This is a scaling exercise, not the measured plant count in the extension capture. The rendering system can collect those transforms, reserve upload space once, and process contiguous work instead of issuing two hundred independently synchronized transfers. The correct unit of change remains one placement; the efficient unit of processing may be a batch. Unreal exposes batch-add and batch-transform operations, and GPU Scene maintains update and upload infrastructure for the resulting primitive and instance data.

There is a less visible problem when an object disappears. Suppose the game destroys the door’s indicator after submitting frame 120, while the GPU is still executing commands that reference the indicator's geometry. Removing the gameplay object is logically immediate, but releasing the memory is a separate operation. Future scene snapshots must stop referring to it. Existing render work must remain valid until its consumers finish. An engine therefore needs deferred destruction, reference ownership, fences, or equivalent lifetime tracking at each boundary. The exact mechanism can vary; the distinction between “no longer part of the scene” and “safe to free” cannot.

Unreal's primitive scene information participates in deferred cleanup, and the scene removal path processes queued render-side removal rather than asking the game thread to delete renderer state in place. GPU resources additionally follow the rendering hardware interface's resource lifetime rules. It would be misleading to turn this into a universal “wait two frames, then delete” rule. Different resources and execution modes can have different outstanding consumers. The source-level points of entry are PrimitiveSceneInfo.h and RendererScene.cpp.

Identity has to survive these transitions. Imagine that indicator A occupied slot 42, was removed, and indicator B later reused slot 42. A delayed update addressed only to “42” could now move the wrong indicator. A common engine-design solution is a generational handle: an index plus a generation counter. If slot 42's generation changes from 7 to 8, an update carrying {42,7} is rejected. This is a proposal we will use for Arda, not a claim that every Unreal primitive identifier uses this exact scheme. Unreal itself distinguishes several identities and indices, which is a warning against treating every integer as interchangeable.

These lifetime rules affect debugging as much as performance. A useful update log can say that object {42,7} changed transform in scene revision 120, its GPU instance range moved during revision 121, and its removal became visible in revision 122. A log that records only a raw buffer offset cannot explain whether an apparent jump came from motion, compaction, or accidental reuse. Good scene representation makes those events distinguishable. The renderer should be able to rearrange storage without changing what object the rest of the engine believes it is addressing.

06The scene becomes GPU data

Increase the leaf density in the room’s planters as a thought experiment: a thousand small placements can fit inside the same room. A CPU could bind each placement’s transform and issue one draw at a time. The captured extension uses a much smaller count, recorded later. That is a useful first renderer, but the submission overhead grows with object count and places the CPU in the middle of every visibility decision. A GPU-driven renderer instead needs the GPU to find object data by an identifier. A draw or a culling result carries an index, and a shader loads the associated transform, bounds, and flags from a scene buffer. This is the purpose of GPU-resident scene data. It is not a GPU copy of every gameplay field.

Unreal calls its management system FGPUScene. Its interfaces update persistent primitive data, upload dynamic primitive data for a view, track dirty primitives, and manage instance allocations. Its buffers distinguish primitive data, instance data, instance payloads, and lightmap data. That division matters: values shared by an entire primitive need not be repeated for every placement, while per-instance variation needs an addressable home. The declarations and separate upload buffers are in GPUScene.h.

FGPUScene: managing shader-readable scene storage
InformationConcrete Unreal data or operationUse in the room
Shared primitive recordsPrimitiveBuffer and PrimitiveUploadBuffer.Upload common state once for the primitive containing the three instanced pots.
Placed instances and optional payloadInstanceSceneDataBuffer, InstancePayloadDataBuffer, upload buffers and allocation/free operations.Address each pot placement and its optional custom or dynamic data.
Lightmap recordsLightmapDataBuffer, its allocator and upload buffer.Provide separately addressed baked-lighting data where the rendering path uses it.
Change tracking and dynamic workAddPrimitiveToUpdate(), Update() and UploadDynamicPrimitiveShaderDataForView().Upload changed persistent records or transient view-generated data without treating the whole scene as new every frame.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: GPUScene.h.

Here “primitive” means a renderer-registered object with common scene properties, not necessarily one triangle. An instanced static mesh component can represent many placements under one primitive. Its common material and mesh relationships can be shared while each instance has its own transform and custom values. A single static mesh component usually presents a much simpler one-placement case. Understanding this distinction prevents a frequent counting error: one actor, one primitive, one mesh section, one instance, and one draw are not guaranteed to be the same unit.

Use a deliberately small example. Use the three pots as our example: one instanced component, three placements of its shared mesh. Give that primitive the illustrative persistent identifier 17. Its current instance allocation begins at entry 400. The entries at 400, 401, and 402 describe the three placements. Each instance record can lead back to primitive 17; the primitive record can identify the range that belongs to it. A visibility pass might produce a list containing only 400 and 402 because the middle pot is hidden. The renderer can then draw the surviving placements without pretending that the second surviving item is the original second instance.

Unreal's shader-side FInstanceSceneData contains the loaded instance ID, current and previous transforms, bounds, a PrimitiveId, relative instance information, payload addressing, and other rendering fields. FPrimitiveSceneData exposes the instance range and shared primitive information. The loader in SceneData.ush interprets the packed representation rather than assuming that a C++ object can be read verbatim by a shader. The shader contract is visible in SceneData.ush; the CPU-side primitive packer is FPrimitiveSceneShaderData.

Crossing from C++ parameters to packed GPU records

These two shader structs are logical values returned by loaders. Their convenient field names do not specify one C++-compatible struct per GPU buffer slot; the packed buffer encoding and optional payload layout remain separate contracts.

Now remove another primitive that precedes our pots in a dense CPU array. The scene may move primitive 17's CPU record from packed position 9 to packed position 8. That is not movement in world space, and it need not mean its persistent primitive identifier changes. Unreal explicitly documents that FPrimitiveSceneInfo::PackedIndex may change when primitives are added or removed. FScene provides a map from persistent primitive indices to packed indices. Meanwhile, an instance allocation can move for its own reasons. Any system caching an offset must participate in relocation or resolve the current offset from a valid handle. See PrimitiveSceneInfo.h and ScenePrivate.h.

The physical buffer layout is an implementation decision underneath this logical model. A structure-of-arrays layout can let adjacent shader lanes read the same field for neighboring instances efficiently. A tiled arrangement may improve locality while controlling allocation overhead. Unreal's current GPU Scene exposes tiled instance-data layout parameters, so it would be inaccurate to present one historical flat record diagram as its permanent byte layout. Our pot example names logical entries and relations; its identifiers and allocation offsets are worked values, not exported GPU addresses. A production implementation must additionally specify alignment, field encoding, precision, and CPU/shader version agreement.

The visibility list itself is the result of several different tests. Frustum culling rejects bounds outside the camera's view volume. Occlusion culling rejects candidates hidden behind other geometry, using a visibility method appropriate to the renderer. Level-of-detail selection chooses how much detail surviving geometry needs at its projected size; it is not the same as deciding whether the object exists. Hierarchical tests can reject a whole group when its enclosing bounds fail. CPU and GPU paths can divide this work differently, but every result is specific to a consumer or view. Our visible list containing 400 and 402 does not authorize deleting instance 401 from shadows or ray tracing.

Updates then become an upload problem. If only the door and character moved, unchanged tiles should retain their data. Dirty ranges or scatter uploads can update selected records. GPU-generated particle data introduces a second writer, so ordering must ensure that simulation has finished before culling or drawing reads it. A render graph is useful here: it records that one pass writes a resource and another reads it, allowing barriers and scheduling to be derived. The persistent scene still owns the meaning and lifetime of the records; the graph owns the frame's work and resource dependencies.

This is the point at which a modular design either becomes clear or begins to collapse. Geometry modules should not hard-code the pot primitive's allocation offset into unrelated material or lighting systems. They should publish renderable data and receive well-defined scene addressing. Shaders should share explicit data-access conventions. Streaming may replace geometry pages without replacing instance identity. Culling may compact visible work without replacing persistent identity. Those separations allow GPU algorithms to evolve while gameplay continues to say “move the door” rather than “rewrite entry 402 of the current visibility buffer.”

07From a proxy to a draw

What a draw asks the GPU to do

Before giving Unreal's intermediate structures names, follow the simplest possible tile through the GPU. A draw is a command to process a particular range of geometry, potentially repeated for several instances, using the currently selected rendering program and state. For our two-triangle tile, an indexed draw can request the six indices [0,1,2,0,2,3]. The GPU fetches the referenced vertices, transforms them toward the camera, determines which image samples the triangles cover, and runs shading work for surviving samples. One draw is therefore neither one triangle nor one pixel. It can generate many triangles and many visible samples.

A shader is a program that runs on the GPU. A shader stage is a particular place where such a program participates in a pipeline. In a conventional raster draw, a vertex shader processes vertex inputs and produces projected positions plus values that later stages can use. Rasterization finds covered samples and interpolates appropriate values across the triangle. A pixel shader evaluates a covered fragment, for example producing surface attributes or color. A compute shader performs general GPU work without requiring this vertex-to-triangle pipeline; culling or deformation can use it and produce buffers that later draws consume. Geometry paths can add or reorganize stages, so this describes our first conventional triangle path.

The program needs inputs. A binding associates a shader input with an actual resource or value: this vertex buffer, that ceramic texture, this material-parameter buffer, or the GPU Scene buffer holding transforms. Render state supplies additional rules, such as whether to reject back-facing triangles, how to compare depth, and whether to blend with an existing color. A shader permutation is a compiled variant selected for a particular combination of features, such as a material with opacity masking and a particular vertex factory. Choosing another variant can change the executable program; changing a tint binding may only change data consumed by the same program.

A pass is a named stage of rendering work with a purpose and resource dependencies. A depth pass finds the nearest accepted surfaces. A base pass evaluates the surface information needed by the selected renderer. A shadow pass observes geometry from a light-related view. A pass can contain many draws, and the same tile can be drawn in more than one pass with different shader variants, bindings, and state. The word pass tells us why work is being done; the word draw names a particular submitted geometry operation. Later we will see exactly what the deferred base pass stores, but we already have enough vocabulary to understand how geometry becomes work.

Finally, indirect arguments are a small GPU-readable record of drawing parameters, such as counts and offsets, consumed by an indirect draw. If GPU culling finds that only eight of ten tiles remain visible, it can write the surviving count and related work data. A later draw reads those arguments without asking the CPU to read back the answer first. This changes who supplies the drawing parameters; it does not change the meaning of a mesh asset, a scene instance, or a material.

Unreal keeps the description separate from the command

We have placed geometry and made its data available to the GPU, but we have not yet said how Unreal turns that information into draw work. The room tile may appear in a depth pass, a shadow pass, the main surface pass, an editor selection pass, and a reflection view. Each consumer needs a different shader combination or render state. If the tile component directly issued a fully specified graphics command, it would either need to know every consumer or force all consumers to accept the same command. Unreal inserts an intermediate description instead.

That description is FMeshBatch. It identifies a vertex factory, a material render proxy, and one or more mesh elements. A mesh element describes such things as the index buffer, first index, triangle count, instance count, and optional indirect arguments. In the simplest tile example, it names our six indices and the data needed to fetch the tile's vertices. The batch is rich enough for a renderer to understand what can be drawn, but it has not yet chosen every pass-specific shader and GPU state. The fields are in MeshBatch.h.

FMeshBatch and FMeshBatchElement: describing drawable work
InformationConcrete Unreal data or operationUse in the room
Batch: geometry interpretationFMeshBatch::VertexFactory selects the geometry-access implementation.Interpret the tile’s static-mesh streams or a character’s supported deformed inputs.
Batch: appearance and elementsMaterialRenderProxy, Elements, primitive topology and pass-policy flags.Associate a section’s material with one or more element descriptions; this is not yet a selected pass shader.
Element: indexed rangeFMeshBatchElement::IndexBuffer, FirstIndex, NumPrimitives, vertex bounds and BaseVertexIndex.For the simple tile, describe two triangles starting at index zero.
Element: repetitions or indirect workNumInstances, optional instance runs, IndirectArgsBuffer and IndirectArgsOffset.Draw compatible tile placements repeatedly, or obtain draw arguments from a GPU buffer on a supported path.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: MeshBatch.h.

The term vertex factory sounds like an object that creates geometry, but its central rendering role is an adapter between a geometry representation and shader inputs. A static mesh can read position and UV buffers. A skinned mesh may fetch bone influences and deformed positions. A particle sprite can derive its corners from particle data and the current view. Material code wants meaningful values such as world position, normal, and texture coordinates regardless of how they were obtained. A vertex factory supplies the geometry-specific machinery and shader integration that makes this possible. The static-mesh case is concrete in LocalVertexFactory.ush.

Geometry access and view relevance are different contracts
TypeInformation it providesUse in the room
FVertexFactoryGetType(), vertex streams/declarations and type-specific shader integration describe how geometry inputs are fetched.A static-mesh and a skinned-mesh path can supply the inputs expected by the material/pass without sharing one buffer layout.
FPrimitiveViewRelevanceFlags including bDrawRelevance, bStaticRelevance, bDynamicRelevance, bShadowRelevance and bRenderInMainPass.Tell a view which kinds of work the primitive can contribute. This is relevance metadata, not a draw command or a final occlusion result.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: VertexFactory.h, PrimitiveViewRelevance.h.

Consider the tile's shadow. If it is opaque and has no vertex displacement, the shadow pass may need little more than positions and transforms. Its color texture is irrelevant. If it is a leaf card whose material rejects transparent pixels, the shadow needs the opacity-mask logic too; otherwise the entire rectangle casts a shadow. If the material moves vertices in wind, the shadow must use a compatible displaced shape. The renderer therefore combines geometry access, material behavior, and the purpose of the pass. “Draw this mesh” is insufficiently precise until those three inputs meet.

FMeshPassProcessor is the abstraction at that meeting point. A concrete pass processor receives mesh batches, determines relevance, chooses shader permutations and state, and builds FMeshDrawCommand records. A mesh draw command contains the information required for submission through the rendering hardware interface, including shader bindings and drawing state. The source describes the processor as transforming descriptions from scene proxies into commands ready for the RHI command list. See MeshPassProcessor.h.

From pass decisions to FMeshDrawCommand
InformationConcrete Unreal data or operationUse in the room

Command: pipeline and dynamic stateCachedPipelineId, StencilRef and PrimitiveType.Record the pipeline-state identity and additional state needed by submission.

Command: primitive addressingPrimitiveIdStreamIndex, together with scene/submission data supplied around the command.Connect an instanced draw to the appropriate scene records. The command is not a complete copy of the world.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: MeshPassProcessor.h, MeshPassProcessor.h.

Unreal also distinguishes work that can be cached from work that must be gathered for the current view. A proxy can submit static elements through DrawStaticElements or gather dynamic elements through GetDynamicMeshElements, subject to its view relevance. In this vocabulary, “static” describes a rendering submission path and caching opportunity; it is not a universal synonym for “the component can never move.” A transform update can often retain geometry and compatible cached commands because the shader reads current scene data through an ID. View-dependent generated geometry may require a different gathering path. The proxy interfaces explain this split in PrimitiveSceneProxy.h.

Caching creates another invalidation obligation. If a command embeds a binding that changes, the cached command must be rebuilt or use an indirection that remains valid. If only an instance transform changes in GPU Scene, a command using that scene data may remain useful. If a material switches from opaque to translucent, the old pass selection is wrong even if the geometry buffer is unchanged. The update categories from the preceding chapter now acquire concrete costs: some touch only data, while others alter the compiled interpretation of that data.

Instancing and indirect drawing fit naturally into this separation. Compatible commands can share state while supplying multiple instance IDs. GPU culling can write an argument buffer containing a surviving instance count, allowing an indirect draw to consume the result without a CPU readback. This does not mean that every Unreal geometry path goes through one identical mesh-command pipeline. Nanite uses specialized visibility and material work, and hair or volume rendering introduces additional paths. The general contract remains valuable: geometry is described independently from the frame's decision about how and where to render it.

For a new engine, the safe extension point is therefore not an unrestricted callback that issues arbitrary GPU commands during scene traversal. It is a representation provider with explicit resources, bounds, material requirements, pass capabilities, and lifetime. The renderer can then schedule the work, validate dependencies, and decide which descriptions can be cached. A low-level escape hatch may still be necessary, but it should not be the only way to add a new geometry type. Otherwise every extension becomes a second renderer with its own inconsistent scene rules.

Count a tiled-floor variant all the way through

As a controlled replacement for a patch of the baseline floor, design one tile-kit actor with three visible components. This is a worked submission plan, not the measured draw count of either capture. Two are ordinary static-mesh components, placing two tiles independently. The third is one instanced-static-mesh component containing ten more tile placements. All twelve placements use the same mesh asset, which has two material sections: ceramic and a metal inset. Assume conventional non-Nanite rasterization, opaque materials, all placements visible, and no additional geometry or editor passes. We will deliberately preserve both section ranges in each of two passes, depth and base, to make the accounting transparent. An optimized Unreal frame may merge, omit, split, or otherwise organize commands differently.

The authoring count is one actor and three mesh-bearing components. Under the ordinary registration path in this example, those components create three primitive proxies and three primitive scene-info records, so the rendering scene has three primitives. The placement count is twelve: one for each ordinary component and ten belonging to the instanced component. There is still only one shared mesh asset and one set of its two section definitions. Section identity describes which triangles use which material binding; it does not become a new actor or a new world placement.

Now count the illustrative draw submissions. Each ordinary component contributes two section draws to each of two passes: 2 components × 2 sections × 2 passes = 8 draws. The instanced component contributes one draw for each section and pass, with each draw processing ten instances: 1 group × 2 sections × 2 passes = 4 draws. The total is twelve draws in this deliberately simple submission plan. Those draws cover 12 placements × 2 sections × 2 passes = 48 placement-section-pass combinations. Instancing grouped work; it did not make nine of the ten tiles cease to exist.

A cached command also does not eliminate that work. It can retain compatible shader choices, bindings, and state so the CPU need not rebuild the same description every frame. The GPU still renders the relevant instances. Moving the seventh instanced tile can update its transform and bounds while leaving shared geometry and compatible cached commands intact. Replacing the metal inset with a translucent material changes pass requirements and invalidates the old opaque interpretation. Removing the instanced component removes one primitive and its ten placements, not ten actors. These different counts explain why optimizing actor count, primitive count, draw count, and triangle count can lead to different decisions.

08Inspect the room as geometry and view-dependent work

The lit image hides both the simplicity of the source geometry and the hierarchy of decisions that makes it visible. Switch the same camera to wireframe. The enclosing walls and the blocks are transformed instances of a cube; they do not become complex geometry merely because indirect light produces detailed gradients on their surfaces. A material, a lighting cache, and a depth discontinuity can create image detail without adding vertices.

Now display bounds. The renderer can reject a component's bound without visiting every triangle. If the bound intersects the view, that is permission to do more work, not proof that all its triangles are visible. The matte block can hide part of the back wall even while both component bounds are inside the camera. A shadow view has different visibility from this camera. The bounds overlay makes the culling input visible; it is not a visualization of every internal culling decision or a measurement of draw count.

The chain to remember is component → proxy behavior → scene membership → GPU-addressable placement → view work. The component owns editable state. The proxy presents a rendering snapshot and geometry-specific behavior. Scene info associates it with the renderer's persistent organization. GPU Scene makes needed data accessible to shaders. The view chooses relevant work. None of these transitions means that the seven UStaticMeshComponent objects are copied byte-for-byte into a GPU buffer.

A depth image is a useful next checkpoint because it contains the result of visible-surface selection without the full lighting solution. The front of the matte block wins where it overlaps the back wall; the back wall remains represented elsewhere. The stored depth convention and the debug view's display mapping are separate matters. For this capture, a native post-process material reads linear SceneDepth in centimeters and divides by 1,000 after tone mapping. Its shader output reaches white at ten meters. This readable display is a custom diagnostic of the actual depth buffer, not raw device Z; do not confuse it with the engine's default depth-view scale.

For Arda, the corresponding debugging feature should expose both levels: human-readable overlays and machine-readable records with units. A bounding-box screenshot answers whether placement is plausible. A bounds export can verify exact values. A depth visualization reveals discontinuities; an untonemapped depth export supports numerical comparisons. Keeping these forms together makes the scene system testable without confusing a display transform with the underlying data.

09The room needs more than static meshes

We can now give every object an identity and a safe route into rendering. The next question is what each object should contain. The room’s floor, a small heightfield exhibit, the walking mannequin, a basin jet, and smoke from an effects station should not all be forced into the same authoring structure merely because they occupy one room. The mannequin and plants are captured additions; the specialist fixtures in the following paragraphs are proposed substitutions or additions, illustrated in the compatibility chapter. We will compare five representations by asking what is stored, how a visible shape is reconstructed, and what a change invalidates. Their concrete Unreal types and feature compatibility are collected later, after the mechanisms have a meaning.

Keep three levels separate as we do this. A file format describes imported data. A geometry representation describes the facts the engine preserves, such as connected vertices, sampled heights, or a density field. A GPU topology describes how a submitted stream assembles into triangles, lines, or points. Unreal's hardware-facing topology definitions include all three, but the presence of a topology does not by itself supply an authoring system, a material interface, or a ray-tracing representation. Those are additional contracts. The topology enum records these low-level choices.

The conventional indexed floor tile remains our reference. Its connectivity and vertex attributes can stay resident while many placements reuse them. The two-section tile variant adds appearance ranges to that connectivity. A Nanite-enabled version can instead store derived cluster and streaming data for its specialized geometry path while retaining the same object identity and material assignments. A cluster is a small group of triangles processed together. Changing the way triangles are stored and selected does not remove the need to know which tile is moving, which material it uses, or which bounds enclose it.

A sampled heightfield reconstructs a floor exhibit

Put a small terrain exhibit on a tray inside the room. Four neighboring samples have heights 0, 0, 10, 10 centimeters, so the patch rises by ten centimeters across a cell. We need not store every horizontal coordinate independently: the grid location supplies those coordinates, and the height sample supplies the vertical coordinate. Connecting neighboring samples reconstructs a triangle surface. Using coarser samples farther away reduces the work while retaining the broad shape. This regularity makes heightfields useful for large terrain.

The saving comes with a restriction. At one horizontal coordinate the heightfield supplies one surface height. An overhanging ledge on the exhibit needs both a lower and an upper surface at some of the same horizontal coordinates; a single ordinary heightfield cannot express that shape. The tray can use a heightfield for its mound and a separate mesh for an overhanging ledge. The two objects can share lighting and visibility infrastructure without sharing their internal geometry format. Selecting a representation is choosing which shapes are cheap to express and which are difficult or impossible.

Unreal Landscape preserves this sampled structure through heightmap data and divides the terrain into components suitable for rendering and updates. Weightmap data answers a different question: how much grass, dirt, or rock should contribute to the material at a location? Raising a height sample changes the surface and its bounds; painting a dirt weight changes appearance without necessarily changing connectivity. That is a concrete reason to keep geometry and material updates separate even inside one specialized terrain system. LandscapeComponent.h exposes the distinct height and weight textures.

The same reconstruction idea appears in specialized heightfield and water producers. A Virtual Heightfield Mesh uses height-related data to generate its renderable surface; a water mesh can provide a surface that wave logic subsequently displaces. They need their own reconstruction and update policies, but the renderer still needs a placed object, conservative bounds, and material requirements. A water surface also needs a lighting and transmission path appropriate to water. Its existence in the main view alone says nothing about whether another subsystem can trace its exact displaced shape.

An indexed surface can change its positions or its connectivity

Place the mannequin on the room’s floor, in front of the matte block. Its triangle connectivity can remain fixed while its vertices move relative to its origin. A skeleton supplies a hierarchy of bone transforms, and skinning weights say how strongly each bone influences each vertex. The current pose reconstructs a new surface from the same reference mesh. A morph target instead stores vertex offsets, so a facial expression changes shape by blending those offsets. Cloth simulation or a mesh deformer can supply further position changes. These mechanisms produce geometry for a particular time; they are not additional world placements of the entire character. Unreal's skeletal-render update interface explicitly carries morph information and current/previous pose policy. See the skeletal render update contract.

Now compare the character's sleeve with the cable along the room’s skirting. A spline-deformed cable can keep its indices and use a curve to reposition the mesh along a path. A skeletal sleeve keeps indices and blends bone-related transforms. A baked Geometry Cache can play recorded shape samples. The authoring inputs and runtime costs differ, but each path must eventually tell its consumers what surface exists now, what it was previously, and what bounds enclose it. If we hide those distinctions under one method called “animate,” a ray consumer cannot know whether it can reuse local geometry, update positions, or needs a different representation.

Cut a hole through the room’s removable wall test panel and the situation changes again. Moving existing vertices is insufficient if the operation introduces new boundaries and triangles. An editable dynamic mesh preserves connectivity that can be modified, then updates its rendering buffers. A procedural mesh producer can instead generate fresh triangle sections from an algorithm. Changes limited to positions may admit partial uploads; changing index connectivity can invalidate section ranges, derived bounds, and acceleration structures. Unreal's dynamic-mesh component deliberately supports partial render updates and internal chunking, which are useful because not every edit should become a full replacement. The dynamic-mesh declaration describes these update facilities.

A fracture adds a third kind of change. The same wall test panel breaks into pieces, each of which may retain its local surface while acquiring a new rigid transform. A Geometry Collection represents those pieces and their simulation relationships. It is wasteful to treat every moving shard as an arbitrary deformation of a single enormous vertex array if the local pieces can be reused. The scene still needs stable ways to address them and a policy for when clustered pieces become independently relevant to rendering. Brush or constructive geometry is yet another authoring route to surfaces or volumes; its editing representation should be converted or interpreted for each consumer rather than mistaken for a universal GPU primitive.

Repetition uses the same separation in the opposite direction. Ten identical floor tiles can share one indexed surface while publishing ten transforms. Foliage can manage many such placements, and an instanced component can store custom values such as tint or wind phase beside each transform. A component's placement order and its current rendering-buffer order may differ, so custom values must follow the correct instance mapping. The source makes that per-instance data explicit. See the instance transform and custom-data records. The useful question is not “is this a static mesh or an effect?” but “which shape data is shared, and which values change per placement or per frame?”

Curves and particles reconstruct a visible surface

Add a small basin to the room’s effects station and let it emit droplets. A simulation can preserve only a position, size, velocity, age, and color for each droplet. To draw a sprite, the renderer constructs corners around the position, often oriented toward the camera, and joins them into triangles. The visible rectangle is reconstructed from a compact record; it need not exist as a persistent authored mesh. Its apparent round droplet shape may come from opacity in a texture. This explains both the efficiency and the limitation: a camera-facing particle can look convincing from the player view while needing a different interpretation for a shadow or a ray query.

A continuous water trail needs a different reconstruction. Store an ordered sequence of particle positions, estimate a direction along the sequence, and build a strip with two sides. Connecting neighboring pairs produces a ribbon. Changing the order can change the visible surface even if the set of point positions is unchanged. Width, facing rules, twisting, and degenerate segments therefore belong to the ribbon contract. A mesh-particle renderer takes another route: it treats each particle transform as a placement of a shared mesh, much like the instanced plant leaves. Unreal provides separate Niagara renderer implementations for these interpretations, confirming that simulation attributes do not prescribe one geometry topology. The sprite renderer is one concrete entry point.

A proposed groom on the room’s mannequin makes the curve interpretation much more demanding. The captured template mannequin has no groom; this is an additional provider to test. A groom can store curves with many points, and simulation guides can control the motion of a much larger set of visible strands. Fine strands require specialized treatment for visibility, light transmission, and shadows. Cards instead approximate groups of hairs using textured surfaces, while a mesh representation can provide a coarser shape. These are alternate representations of the same intended appearance, not three interchangeable storage encodings with identical results. The chosen representation changes cost, silhouette, transparency, and supported platforms. Epic describes this reconstruction pipeline and its alternatives in Groom Scalability and Performance.

Our skirting cable, basin ribbon, and mannequin hair all begin with curve-like information, yet none can be rendered correctly by a generic instruction saying only “draw curve.” The cable reconstructs a substantial indexed surface around a path. The ribbon reconstructs an oriented strip. Hair uses many thin strands and a dedicated shading treatment. A useful geometry interface names the generated attributes, bounds, history, and consumer capabilities. The mathematical similarity of the inputs does not establish identical renderer support.

Point samples describe observations, not connectivity

Suppose we scan the room with LiDAR. The result can be a set of measured positions and colors, perhaps with additional attributes, without indices connecting neighboring samples into triangles. A point renderer can draw visible marks or finite footprints for those samples. From a distance, sufficiently dense marks can suggest a continuous wall. Up close, holes and uneven sampling may reveal that the surface was never actually reconstructed. The apparent continuity in the image is not proof of watertight geometry.

The distinction matters when the camera approaches the scanned door or a reflection ray needs to intersect it. We must decide what a point means geometrically: an infinitesimal sample, a billboard, a disk, a sphere, or evidence used by a surface-reconstruction algorithm. Each answer creates different silhouettes and intersections. Building a triangle mesh from the scan introduces assumptions about how samples connect; it is a derived product with its own revision and quality. Unreal's LiDAR Point Cloud plugin supplies importing, processing, and rendering, but its presence does not automatically turn every scan into every other geometry representation. Epic's plugin description identifies that scope.

A collision sphere and a signed distance field reinforce the same lesson. They can be excellent descriptions for their intended queries while providing no ordinary shaded surface to the main raster path by themselves. A mathematical implicit surface needs an explicit tracing or conversion implementation. Registering a producer should therefore declare what it can deliver, rather than inherit a claim of complete support from a broad label such as “primitive.” We will use exactly this failure case when designing an Arda point provider.

A volume describes matter along the whole ray

The final proposed fixture is mist above the room’s basin. A surface tells us where a boundary is. A volume can tell us how much matter exists at points throughout a region. Consider a ray crossing one meter of uniform absorbing mist with extinction coefficient 2 m−1. In a simple absorption-only model, its surviving fraction is exp(−2 × 1) ≈ 0.135. There need not be a single opaque triangle at which the ray stops. Several portions of the path contribute to attenuation, and scattering or emission can add light along that path.

A ray marcher approximates this integral by taking samples along the ray. If the density changes with position, it accumulates the contributions of those local samples. Smaller steps can recover more detail at higher cost; empty regions invite skipping or sparse storage. A Sparse Volume Texture stores volumetric attributes while avoiding a fully dense allocation for unused regions. Its animated frames can describe evolving smoke. Unlike a particle sprite with a painted smoke image, the data describes a three-dimensional field whose result can change coherently with the viewing direction.

Unreal's heterogeneous-volume path combines a volume-domain material with such data. The material describes how sampled values affect the volume's optical properties, while the component provides placement and playback state. A bounding region tells the renderer where integration may be required. A density edit, a playback-frame change, and moving the whole volume are different updates, just as topology, deformation, and rigid movement were different for meshes. This remains an experimental feature with configuration-dependent support, as described in Heterogeneous Volumes; the component integration is visible in the component declaration.

We have five ways to obtain visible matter: reconstruct a sampled height surface, fetch and possibly deform connected vertices, reconstruct surfaces or strands from curves and particles, display or reconstruct point samples, and integrate a field through space. The shared scene contract does not require their internals to be identical. It requires an identity, appropriate placement, conservative bounds, explicit resources and updates, and truthful declarations of what each consumer can do. The compatibility comparison later in the article is useful precisely because main-view visibility, shadowing, hardware rays, software distance-field tracing, and cached indirect lighting are separate questions.

10Motion is more than a matrix

Return to the door and write its transformation carefully. A local position belongs to the mesh's coordinate system. The hinge contributes a relative transform, the door actor contributes a world placement, and the camera contributes a world-to-view transform followed by projection. In this article's mathematical convention we use column vectors, so the composition is pclip = P V M plocal. Unreal's matrix APIs and shader helpers have their own conventions; the equation describes the sequence, not an instruction to paste this multiplication order into arbitrary engine code. The important fact is that object placement and observation are separate operations.

A numerical example makes attachment less mysterious. Put the hinge at world (−150,200,0) cm, ahead of the glossy block. A point at the door’s lower far corner lies at local (100,0,0). At zero yaw it is at (−50,200,0). A ninety-degree rotation around the vertical axis maps that offset to (0,100,0), placing it at (−150,300,0). The attached indicator is at hinge-relative (60,0,150), so its center moves from (−90,200,150) to (−150,260,150). These are the extension’s measured attachment coordinates. We resolve the world transforms before rendering; the GPU needs the resolved placement, not a recursive walk through the actor’s attachment tree.

Normals require care when scale is nonuniform. A direction perpendicular to a surface before scaling must remain perpendicular afterward. Multiplying it by the same matrix as a position does not generally preserve that condition. The usual mathematical transformation uses the inverse transpose of the linear part, followed by normalization. Tangents and orientation signs also matter, especially for mirrored instances. Unreal's shader-side instance data includes inverse-transform and scale-related information because geometry interpretation needs more than three translation values. These fields are visible in SceneData.ush.

Skinning introduces transforms inside the object. Zoom into a small teaching strip representing the mannequin’s sleeve; these are illustrative local values, not exported bone weights from the template asset. Let a vertex be influenced by two bones with weights 0.75 and 0.25. The reference pose is the undeformed pose in which the mesh was authored. For each influencing bone, the inverse of its reference transform first converts the mesh point into that bone’s reference coordinates; the current bone transform then moves that point into the posed mesh. After this pair of operations, suppose the two candidate positions are (2,0,0) and (2,4,0). Linear blend skinning gives 0.75 × (2,0,0) + 0.25 × (2,4,0) = (2,1,0). The component's world transform places this deformed local point into the room. The weights sum to one so the interpolation retains the expected affine behavior. Normals and tangents require corresponding deformation and normalization policies.

A morph changes the input shape through weighted deltas, while cloth or a deformer can supply another position result. The engine has to define the ordering and source of these operations for a particular path. “Animation” is therefore not one field in the scene record. It is a process that produces geometry state and sometimes bounds, with explicit resources and frame dependencies. Unreal's skeletal rendering interfaces distinguish current and previous bone data and expose morph updates. A skin cache can materialize deformed results for reuse by consumers, rather than forcing every pass to repeat all deformation work. The relevant interfaces begin in SkeletalRenderPublic.h.

The room mannequin’s deformation handoff
TypeInformation or operation it providesUse and lifetime
USkinnedMeshComponentComponent-space pose access through GetComponentSpaceTransforms(), previous transform storage, and a MeshObject reference.The character has a pose inside the mesh in addition to the component’s placement in the room.
FSkeletalMeshObjectUpdate() accepts dynamic mesh/morph data and a previous-bone-update policy; geometry paths expose GetSkinVertexFactory() and reference-to-local matrices.Carry rendering-facing deformation data into the supported skinning path. Matrix views returned from dynamic data must not be retained across frames.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: SkinnedMeshComponent.h, SkinnedMeshComponent.h, SkeletalRenderPublic.h.

Why retain the previous state? Temporal antialiasing, temporal upscaling, motion blur, and temporal lighting filters need to connect this frame's surface sample to the prior frame. A motion vector describes how a surface point moved on screen. It depends on the current and previous object transforms, deformation states, and camera transforms. A stationary door can have nonzero screen motion when the camera moves. A sleeve on the mannequin can move while its component transform stays constant. Storing only an actor velocity cannot describe either case fully.

Bounds must follow the same physical reality. If the character's hand extends beyond a reference-pose box, a culling system using that box may remove visible geometry. If wind displacement moves a leaf beyond its advertised bounds, the leaf can disappear near the edge of a view or cast an incomplete shadow. Excessively enlarged bounds avoid some missing geometry but make culling less effective and may increase shadow work. Bounds are thus both a correctness contract and a performance parameter. Unreal updates primitive bounds during transform propagation, while specialized geometry paths must account for their own deformation.

Large worlds add precision to the representation problem. As a precision test, translate the entire room far from the world origin while preserving every relative placement. A local vertex can retain fine detail near its asset origin while an object’s world position has a very large magnitude. Converting everything to one ordinary single-precision world-space buffer too early loses that advantage. Unreal's large-world rendering code uses representations and relative-coordinate techniques suited to the particular stage; the instance shader types include double-float matrix forms. Arda does not need to copy every encoding immediately, but it should define coordinate spaces at interfaces and avoid making an unexamined global float transform the only possible representation.

The same principles apply to a teleport. The object changes location, but preserving a long motion vector from its old location can smear history across the screen. A spawn has no meaningful previous observation; a camera cut invalidates view history; a topology change may break correspondence between vertices. A scene update needs a way to express discontinuity and history validity, rather than relying on every downstream temporal effect to infer it. The proposal for Arda will treat previous state and invalidation as part of the scene contract from the beginning.

11Add the door, plants, and mannequin—and follow their state

The baseline established asset sharing with seven simple cube components. Now keep those seven placements and the ceiling RectLight, and add the objects whose contracts we have just derived. This is an actual extension of the saved room, stored as /Game/Labs/SceneRepresentationRoom. The original /Game/Labs/LumenRoom remains the baseline for the material-buffer and Lumen experiments. The exported inventory, camera and pose report, and asset and source provenance record this experiment. Runtime object paths retain the loaded baseline package name; the extension is saved separately. All new screenshots are 1280 × 720 with fixed exposure EV100 = 4; they preserve the renderer’s stochastic lighting noise.

The new actors have distinct jobs. A door and its attached indicator demonstrate inherited rigid motion. Three small plants demonstrate shared meshes with many instance transforms. A template mannequin demonstrates a changing skeletal pose inside one component. The following captures use Unreal's renderer; the plant silhouettes, attachment, and animation are implemented in components rather than painted into a diagram.
