Count at the right level. The additions use three instanced components, two door-assembly mesh components, and one skeletal mesh component. The three instanced components contain thirty placements in total: three pots, three stems, and twenty-four leaves. That is six added primitive-bearing components, not thirty-six actors and not a measured draw count. Sections, passes, culling, and renderer-specific paths determine the work that eventually reaches the GPU. The earlier twelve-tile accounting exercise was a deliberately controlled submission plan; it is not an estimate of this captured frame.

One set of leaf buffers, twenty-four placements

The plants sit at UE X = −145, −105, and −65 cm, with Y = 80 cm, near the open front of the room. The detail camera below moves closer to them; the overview camera above stays fixed. The broad leaf outline comes from the material's opacity mask on a card. The wireframe reveals the triangles that supply that mask's sampling domain. A mask can remove covered samples from a rectangle without introducing additional silhouette vertices into its underlying mesh.

This is the concrete meaning of the GPU Scene example with three pot placements. Shared primitive-level state identifies compatible geometry and policy; instance-level records identify the individual placements. The illustrative indices 17 and 400–402 in the earlier diagram explain addressing. They were not extracted from this capture's private GPU allocations. The actual instance counts and transforms are exported instead, so the explanation never relies on guessing those indices.

Move the hinge; keep the door mesh

The hinge is at (−150,200,0) cm. A 100 cm wide, 200 cm high door starts along +X and rotates through +90° yaw toward +Y. Its six-centimeter thickness clears the baseline blocks. The indicator starts at hinge-relative (60,0,150), so its center travels from (−90,200,150) to (−150,260,150). Compare these values with the earlier attachment diagram: the computed example and the captured hierarchy now describe the same object.

At the scene boundary, this edit is a transform change with consequences for bounds, current/previous placement, visibility, and supported secondary representations. It is not a request to rewrite the door's indices. The emissive indicator may contribute through supported lighting paths, but its presence creates no additional point or rect light component. Adding such a component would be a separate scene-service contribution, as the light chapter explains.

Change a pose inside one placed object

The mannequin stands at (65,110,0) cm, in front of the matte block. The two images below evaluate ThirdPersonWalk at 0.10 s and 0.45 s, keeping the actor at the same location and −90° yaw. We can therefore isolate a deformation update from a rigid placement update. The template mesh and animation are actual Unreal assets; the two-bone sleeve strip earlier in the essay is a small arithmetic model of the same kind of operation, not a claim about this asset's particular weights.

A real-time implementation must retain a coherent previous pose and placement when it emits motion. It must also supply bounds that enclose the deformed surface and negotiate which shadow and ray paths can consume that geometry. Merely seeing the mannequin in a lit image does not establish that software distance fields or a particular GI cache represent its moving triangles. The baseline distance-field and card captures later in the essay remain explicitly about the seven rigid cube components.

Inspect the extended scene without its final lighting

We have now used the same room to distinguish asset sharing, component registration, instance placement, attachment, deformation, surface inputs, and conservative extent. The next chapters return to its baseline material and lighting comparisons. The compatibility fixtures at the end extend this room's test vocabulary—heightfields, mutable topology, particles, hair, scans, and volumes—without pretending that all those providers are already implemented by the six additions above.

12A material is a surface program

The captured room begins with constant surface parameters: neutral walls and floor, a rough matte block, and a smooth metallic block. To understand a more general surface program, replace our teaching floor patch with a textured ceramic tile. Its proposed graph samples a color texture, a normal map, and a roughness texture, and can blend wear through a painted mask. This is a material variant of the same floor location; it is not present in the baseline captures. The graph computes surface properties. It does not contain the final color of the tile, which also depends on illumination, shadows, reflections, the camera, and exposure.

A useful conceptual function is surface = Material(geometry inputs, parameters, textures). Geometry inputs include position, normal, tangent frame, UVs, vertex colors, and optional instance data. Parameters include a tint or roughness multiplier. The output describes how the surface interacts with light: base color, roughness, metallic behavior, emission, and the other properties allowed by the chosen material model. A bidirectional reflectance distribution function, usually abbreviated BRDF, describes the directional response of a surface to incoming light. The material supplies the values and model needed to evaluate that response.

For example, the ceramic tile can sample a texture value (0.4,0.3,0.2) and multiply it by a tint (0.8,1.0,0.8), producing (0.32,0.30,0.16) in the example's working color space. That value is still a surface color parameter, not the final pixel. A white light illuminating it from above and a red light at grazing incidence can produce different outgoing radiance. The normal map changes the local shading orientation, while the underlying triangle remains flat unless another mechanism changes geometry. This separation explains how a surface can appear detailed without adding silhouette detail.

Unreal distinguishes the authored material, its compiled rendering resources, and the render proxy through which parameters and resources are accessed. UMaterial and material-instance objects belong to the authoring-facing world. FMaterial and FMaterialResource participate in the compiled rendering side. FMaterialRenderProxy supplies the renderer-facing material access and maintains uniform-expression caches. A mesh batch refers to a material render proxy, rather than executing a material graph by walking editor nodes for every pixel. The resource types are in MaterialShared.h, and the proxy and caches are in MaterialRenderProxy.h.

Material types: authored choices, compiled behavior and bound values
TypeInformation it providesUse in the room
UMaterialAuthored material/expression data and settings such as MaterialDomain and BlendMode.Define the ceramic-tile computation and whether it describes an opaque surface or another domain/path.
UMaterialInstanceParent plus scalar, vector and texture parameter overrides; static parameters can select compiled variants.Keep one parent material while tinting one tile or selecting a different texture.
FMaterialCompiled-material interface: domain, blending and shading-model queries, shader maps and compilation/rendering resources.Let pass selection ask which shading behavior and shader variants the tile material supports.
FMaterialResourceA concrete FMaterial implementation for material/material-instance resources and their feature/quality configuration.Represent the compiled tile resource for the rendering configuration; it is not a placed scene object.
FMaterialRenderProxyGetMaterialWithFallback(), parameter lookup and UniformExpressionCache.A mesh batch resolves a usable compiled material and the current values needed to bind it.
FUniformExpressionCacheMaterial uniform buffers, allocated virtual-texture references, parameter-collection IDs and the shader-map identity used for the cache.Reuse uniform evaluation and bindings for the tile. Changing parameters may invalidate this cache without changing the tile mesh.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: Material.h, MaterialInstance.h, MaterialInstance.h, MaterialShared.h, MaterialShared.h, MaterialRenderProxy.h.

Material instances reuse a parent material while changing selected parameters. Ten tiles can share one compiled surface program and use different tint values or texture bindings. A dynamic material instance lets gameplay change appropriate runtime parameters. Static switches are different: they affect which code is compiled and can create distinct shader variants. Confusing these categories leads to poor architecture. A runtime color change should not require regenerating geometry, while a change that selects a different compiled branch cannot always be represented by overwriting one float.

Material slots connect a mesh's sections to its appearance. Suppose the proposed indoor basin has section zero for ceramic and section one for brass. The asset supplies default materials, while a placed component can override them. Neither arrangement requires embedding a complete material program into each vertex. Section data selects a material binding; vertex data supplies the geometric inputs that the chosen program consumes. The same brass material may appear on the door handle and the basin drain despite their geometry coming from different assets.

Material domains and blending choices also affect where work belongs. An opaque surface can contribute a nearest visible surface and usually write depth. A masked material either accepts or rejects a covered sample based on an opacity threshold, as demonstrated by the room’s captured leaf cards. A translucent material requires compositing contributions through or over other surfaces. A volume-domain material describes participating matter rather than a thin boundary. A decal modifies the appearance of another surface, and a post-process material operates on image-space inputs. Treating all of these as interchangeable “materials on a triangle” would hide essential renderer contracts.

Vertex displacement crosses the boundary between appearance and geometry. Unreal's world-position-offset material logic can move vertices, such as making leaves sway. The program is authored as material behavior, but the consequences include bounds, shadows, previous positions, and ray-tracing compatibility. A material system must therefore report relevant capabilities to the geometry and pass systems. Opacity masking has a similar effect on coverage. The pass processor cannot choose a cheap opaque depth shader if the material's holes determine which samples exist.

Unreal also supports richer material representations such as Substrate, so the familiar list of base color, metallic, and roughness should be understood as an accessible starting model rather than a permanent complete schema for every shading path. The architectural requirement is broader: the renderer and material compiler agree on a surface representation, the allowed operations, and the consumers that can evaluate or store it. A modular scene system should refer to a material program and its binding data while allowing that representation to evolve. It should not hard-code the editor's node graph into every geometry provider.

13A visible surface becomes a lit pixel

Return to the baseline room and its ceiling RectLight. The light has a world position, a color, an intensity, and a spatial shape describing where it sends light. These properties belong to the light, while the floor’s roughness and color belong to the surface. Keeping them separate is what lets one light illuminate many materials and one material respond to many lights. In Unreal, light components create renderer-facing light state, analogous in purpose to the primitive handoff but using light-specific types. FLightSceneProxy provides rendering properties and specialized behavior for lights. The integration begins in LightComponent.cpp and LightSceneProxy.h.

The light has its own proxy and scene-info record
InformationConcrete Unreal data or operationUse in the room
FLightSceneProxy: light propertiesLightToWorld, position/color getters, light-type-specific radius/source-shape queries and shadow policy.Describe where the light sends light and how the renderer should handle its supported shadow behavior.
FLightSceneProxy: specialized operationsVirtual light-parameter and shadow-initializer operations supplied by concrete light types.A point light and a directional light share scene integration while producing different lighting/shadow work.
FLightSceneInfo: scene membershipProxy, Id, Scene, OctreeId, interaction-list heads and precomputed-lighting validity state.Integrate the light with renderer lookup and applicable light/primitive interactions. It does not store every object’s final illumination.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: LightSceneProxy.h, LightSceneInfo.h.

A directional light approximates a distant source whose incoming direction is effectively shared across the scene. A point light emits around a position. A spot light restricts emission to a cone. A rect light describes an area-shaped source with the implementation's supported approximations. A sky light represents environmental illumination rather than an ordinary local bulb. Their shadowing and performance characteristics differ. The common requirement is that the renderer can obtain the incident-light direction and contribution relevant to a surface point, then evaluate the material's response.

To make that point concrete, suppose the tile faces upward and the light lies above it. A diffuse response includes the cosine between the surface normal and the incoming-light direction. If the normal and direction align, the cosine factor is one; if the light grazes the tile at sixty degrees from the normal, it is one half. A rough dielectric surface also has a specular response determined by its material model. Distance attenuation and the light's intensity affect the arriving illumination. These computations evaluate lighting; sampling the tile texture evaluates the surface. A deferred renderer separates much of that work.

Rasterization first answers a geometric question: which projected triangles cover each sample? Depth testing determines which accepted surface is closest for an opaque view. Interpolation supplies values such as UVs and normals at the covered sample. The material then evaluates the visible surface's properties. In a conventional deferred path, those properties are encoded in several screen-sized render targets collectively called the GBuffer, short for geometry buffer. Depth is typically stored separately and can help reconstruct position. The buffers contain a description suitable for later lighting, not a complete copy of the original mesh.

Unreal's FGBufferData exposes a logical decoded representation with fields such as world normal, base color, metallic, roughness, shading-model identity, and other data used by supported shading paths. The actual texture packing depends on configuration and feature choices; the logical structure is not a declaration that every field occupies a separate full-precision texture. This distinction is important when extending a renderer: the surface contract and the storage encoding are related but separate designs. The decoded structure is in DeferredShadingCommon.ush.

FGBufferData: decoded surface information for one sample
InformationConcrete Unreal data or operationUse in the room
Surface orientationWorldNormal and, for supported paths, other orientation data.The lighting calculation knows which way this floor sample faces.
Reflectance parametersBaseColor, Metallic, Specular and Roughness.Distinguish the rough matte block from the smoother metallic block at the same illumination.
Model selection and extensionsShadingModelID and CustomData with model-dependent meaning.Choose how to interpret extra surface information and evaluate the supported lighting response.
Depth and ancillary dataDepth, custom-depth/stencil-related values and other decoded inputs.Locate or classify the visible sample alongside its material properties.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: DeferredShadingCommon.ush.

This is a shader-side value for a surface sample, not a persistent per-object record. It is also not a universal storage schema for every rendering mode: translucent and richer material paths can require other contracts, and decoded values need not each occupy their own GBuffer texture.

As another explicit room variant, attach a point light to the door’s indicator; the captured indicator itself is only a mesh. Now the floor has a second light to evaluate. The tile texture generally does not need to be sampled from scratch once per light in the deferred opaque lighting stage. The renderer reads the stored surface attributes, evaluates the second light, and adds its contribution. For an illustrative pixel, the first light might contribute (0.12,0.10,0.06) and the second (0.02,0.03,0.05) in linear scene-referred RGB, giving (0.14,0.13,0.11) before other illumination and processing. These are invented values to show accumulation. Lighting is not performed by multiplying already tone-mapped display colors.

The approach has costs. Multiple render targets consume memory bandwidth, and a fixed encoding limits which surface information can be retained. A one-layer nearest-surface description cannot by itself represent arbitrary stacks of transparent surfaces. Specialized shading models may need additional data or passes. The reason to use deferred shading is therefore not that it is universally simpler. It makes a particular tradeoff: spend bandwidth on a reusable description of visible surfaces, then organize lighting largely independently of the original geometry submissions.

Shadows add another visibility question. The light illuminates a point only if the relevant path to the source is unobstructed, subject to the chosen shadow approximation. A shadow map renders depth from a light-related view and compares the shaded point against that stored depth. Unreal also has Virtual Shadow Maps and ray-traced shadow paths under appropriate configurations. A tight camera aimed at the floor can exclude the matte block while that block still obstructs the ceiling light. Main-view culling must therefore not erase the block from the persistent scene merely because it is not directly visible. Shadow consumers decide their own relevant work.

Opacity and deformation must agree across those consumers. A masked leaf casts a cutout shadow only if the shadow path evaluates its coverage correctly. A wind-deformed planter leaf casts a convincing shadow only if the shadow geometry represents the appropriate deformation. The exact performance compromise can vary with distance or quality settings, but the system needs a declared relationship between the representations. This is another reason to keep material requirements, geometry capabilities, and scene updates explicit rather than burying them inside one main-view draw callback.

The proposed basin spray demonstrates the limits of one opaque surface record. A translucent droplet or smoke sprite contributes through a compositing operation that depends on what is behind it. Such work often follows separate lighting and compositing paths, with sorting and order-independent techniques available for particular cases. Hair strands and participating volumes introduce their own visibility and accumulation. Deferred decals can modify receiving surfaces through decal-specific buffers or later operations. Post-processing then consumes rendered images to implement effects such as bloom, depth of field, exposure, and tone mapping. These are consumers and transformations of scene results, not extra geometry attributes that should be copied into every primitive.

The actual Unreal frame is more involved than a straight list of “geometry, lights, transparency.” The deferred renderer interleaves preparation, shadow work, surface rendering, indirect illumination, reflections, specialized effects, and post-processing, with dependencies and optional paths. FDeferredShadingSceneRenderer::Render shows calls for the base pass, diffuse indirect lighting, lights, translucency, and hair-related lighting. Its render graph describes resource access so work can be scheduled safely. We use a simplified sequence to explain causality; the implementation is a graph of dependent work rather than a fixed textbook conveyor belt. See the base-pass scheduling, lighting work, and translucency work in DeferredShadingRenderer.cpp.

Inspect the surface separately from its illumination

To reproduce the distinction, open the saved /Game/Labs/LumenRoom baseline and keep its camera fixed. Inspect the matte block and the floor: they already have simple opaque materials with constant roughness and no world-position offset. In the viewport's View Mode menu, open Buffer Visualization and inspect Base Color, World Normal, Roughness, and Scene Depth one at a time. The exact labels are registered in the engine visualization configuration. These modes expose different intermediate values at the same visible surface rather than four alternative final looks.

Change the ceiling RectLight’s intensity and color while keeping the geometry and camera fixed. The Lit result should change as illumination changes; the simple material's Base Color and Roughness should not change merely because the light moved. Rotate the matte block in a separate experiment, and the World Normal view should change orientation. Then use viewmode wireframe on this conventional mesh to inspect its edges and viewmode lit to return. These commands are documented in Viewport Modes. The experiment gives a practical debugging fork: incorrect Base Color points toward material inputs; correct surface data with unexpected Lit output points toward lighting, visibility, or later processing.

For a bounds check, open the extension map /Game/Labs/SceneRepresentationRoom, enable Show → Advanced → Bounds in the editor viewport, and inspect the room mannequin while changing its pose or its advertised bounds. Bounds is a registered advanced show flag. A visible surface outside its bound is a correctness warning; a very large bound enclosing a small surface explains why culling may be ineffective. This is an observation exercise rather than a demand to reduce every bound aggressively: the bound must still enclose the geometry in all supported poses.

14Separate the room's surfaces from the light they reflect

Return from the extension to the baseline’s seven components. They produce several useful per-pixel descriptions. First examine base color. It answers what material property the winning surface supplies, before indirect illumination makes the neutral floor appear tinted. The red wall's material and the red light reflected onto the floor are different quantities. The floor keeps its neutral base color even where its final lit appearance becomes red. This is the concrete reason deferred rendering separates surface evaluation from lighting evaluation.

The world-normal view answers a different question: which way does the visible surface face? Identical materials on the floor and back wall do not imply identical illumination, because their normals differ. Under nonuniform scale, transform normals with the inverse transpose of the linear transform and normalize them. The derivation follows from perpendicularity. For a tangent vvv, nTv=0n^Tv=0nTv=0. After transforming the tangent to AvAvAv, choose n′=A−Tnn'=A^{-T}nn′=A−Tn, giving (n′)TAv=nTv=0(n')^TAv=n^Tv=0(n′)TAv=nTv=0. Multiplying a normal by AAA as if it were a position does not preserve this relation for general nonuniform scale.

The matte block uses roughness 0.7 and metallic 0; the glossy block uses roughness 0.12 and metallic 0.85. Roughness changes the distribution of reflection directions, while metallic changes how base color and reflectance participate in the shading model. These values are shader inputs, not labels such as “reflective object” stored on the actor. A low-roughness surface requires sharper directional information from the reflection system than a rough diffuse surface does.

These views are selections of shading inputs, not an exhaustive description of the engine's packed GBuffer layout. The layout can depend on material features and renderer settings. What survives those implementation choices is the contract: visible-surface evaluation makes material properties available, and lighting uses them with positions, normals, light data, shadows, and indirect-light estimates. The light component is not another material slot on each wall. It contributes illumination to relevant receivers through renderer light data and lighting passes.

The ceiling light in this capture is a movable RectLightComponent with 2,400 lumens, source width 130 cm, source height 120 cm, and attenuation radius 2,000 cm. It is placed at (0,270,298) cm and points downward. Exposure is held fixed for the capture sequence. These settings make the experiment reproducible, but the image is not a radiometric comparison with the CPU lab: the reduced renderer uses its own normalized radiance units, while Unreal applies its light-unit conventions, shading, reconstruction, exposure, and display pipeline.

15The camera does not see the whole lighting problem

The ceiling area light reaches the floor directly. The floor also receives light that first struck the room’s red wall. That second contribution is indirect illumination: the direction and color of arriving light depend on other surfaces. The glossy block reflects parts of the room outside the camera’s first-hit image. Both effects ask questions that the nearest visible surface at each screen pixel cannot fully answer. This is where the persistent scene and the GBuffer must be kept conceptually separate. The GBuffer describes what this camera currently sees; the scene describes the world that other visibility and lighting queries may need.

A screen-space trace can search depth and other buffers to find a candidate intersection along a projected ray. It is attractive because those buffers already exist and match the visible rasterized geometry closely. But if the red wall is outside the image, its samples are absent. The same problem occurs for surfaces hidden behind the first depth layer. A purely screen-space method cannot recover information that was never stored. Temporal reuse can improve stability and coverage over time, but it does not turn one current image into a complete three-dimensional world.

Hardware ray tracing uses acceleration structures to make three-dimensional intersection queries efficient. A bottom-level acceleration structure, or BLAS, organizes the geometry of an object or geometry group. A top-level acceleration structure, or TLAS, organizes placed instances with their transforms. This resembles the asset-versus-placement distinction with which we began, now specialized for ray traversal. Moving a rigid door can change an instance transform while reusing its local geometry structure. Deforming a character can require updating or rebuilding geometry data as well. Unreal's ray-tracing scene implementation manages instance data and top-level builds in RayTracingScene.cpp.

A ray intersection is only part of a lighting answer. It tells us that a ray met some geometry at a distance, with information identifying the hit. We still need a surface response and an estimate of illumination at that location. Evaluating the full original material and tracing enough additional rays for every query can be too expensive for a real-time budget. A lighting system therefore chooses representations and caches appropriate to the question. This does not make the cached answer identical to the full path-traced solution; it makes the approximation explicit and affordable.

Lumen uses a combination of tracing and lighting representations. Depending on configuration, it can combine screen traces with software tracing through distance-field representations or hardware ray tracing. A signed distance field stores an estimate of distance to a surface throughout space, allowing a ray to advance according to distance estimates instead of testing all triangles. This representation has its own resolution and shape limitations. Hardware tracing addresses a different geometry representation and has its own update costs. Neither path should be described as “just read the GBuffer for everything.” Epic's Lumen Technical Details explains the configurable tracing paths and their limitations.

Lumen's Surface Cache captures material-related surface information using parameterizations associated with mesh cards, then maintains lighting information useful to indirect queries. A card is an oriented capture representation of part of a surface, not a replacement gameplay object and not simply the final camera GBuffer saved forever. Coverage matters: an interior corner or poorly represented region can have different behavior from a simple exterior wall. The renderer must also respond when the object, its material, or the lighting changes. FLumenSceneData maintains specialized scene data alongside the ordinary renderer scene; its declaration is in LumenSceneData.h.

FLumenSceneData: a maintained representation for indirect-lighting queries
InformationConcrete Unreal data or operationUse in the room

Captured surface dataAlbedoAtlas, NormalAtlas, EmissiveAtlas and DepthAtlas.Retain material/shape samples from card captures; these are not the player camera’s current GBuffer.

The progression is now concrete: a component authors a change, its rendering representation exposes usable state, scene records organize it, and specialized consumers maintain derived data. The tables identify the information at each boundary; the surrounding walkthrough explains why that boundary exists.

Follow one indirect-light sample in the room conceptually. A visible floor sample provides a position and surface orientation. A lighting algorithm selects an incoming direction to investigate. A trace finds the red wall, perhaps through a representation other than the main-view triangles. A lighting lookup or hit evaluation estimates the radiance returning from that wall. The floor material’s response weights the arriving light, and temporal or spatial filtering stabilizes the estimate under the available sample budget. The exact Lumen pipeline is more sophisticated, but each step now has an understandable responsibility: find a surface, know its appearance and illumination, transport a contribution, and control sampling noise.

This is also why “the object is visible” does not establish that it participates correctly in GI. A procedural mesh can be rasterized by a custom proxy without supplying the representation a particular software tracing path needs. A volume or particle effect may use a separate lighting solution. Material displacement can differ from a fallback ray geometry. Nanite can render extremely detailed visible geometry while another consumer uses a selected fallback or supported specialized ray representation. Compatibility must be tested per consumer and configuration. A scene architecture should represent missing capabilities explicitly, not assume that successful main-view rendering proves universal support.

Unreal's static mesh LOD resources themselves reveal the coexistence of representations: alongside sections and mesh resources are references for distance-field data, card-representation data, and ray-tracing geometry. Those fields may be absent when not available. This is strong evidence for a modular design centered on one object identity with several optional derived products. The fields are declared together in StaticMeshResources.h. Sharing identity allows changes to invalidate the right products; separating products allows each algorithm to use a form suited to its work.

Real-time GI also adds temporal lifetimes. A lighting cache may persist longer than one frame, refine incrementally, and be invalidated by movement, material changes, or lighting changes. A new light might produce visible direct illumination before every cached indirect contribution has fully converged. A scene system should expose enough revision information for consumers to make these decisions. The renderer's graph can order this frame's updates, but it cannot invent the semantic fact that a cached wall capture became stale because the material changed. Scene representation must carry that cause to the lighting subsystem.

Test the representation that a lighting query actually uses

In the baseline room, keep the original camera and choose View Mode → Lumen → Overview. Follow the matte block’s silhouette and the floor-wall corner across the available views. Then choose the Surface Cache visualization and look for magenta coverage gaps on surfaces that are visible in Lit mode. The observation narrows the problem to capture coverage; increasing the main-view triangle count alone does not explain or repair it. Investigate the mesh's structure and capture settings, and compare again after the relevant data has rebuilt.

Open the console and enter r.Lumen.Visualize.CardPlacement 1 to show the capture-card arrangement around the room’s separate walls and blocks; enter the same command with 0 to turn the overlay off. The local source registers this switch in LumenVisualize.cpp. The floor-wall corner and each block’s flat faces can require different capture directions even when all look detailed in the normal camera. Inspecting the cards connects an artifact to the particular approximation that produced it.

A second controlled test separates screen information from other tracing data. First query r.Lumen.ScreenProbeGather.ScreenTraces in the console and note its existing value. Temporarily set it to 0, keep the camera and lighting fixed, and compare diffuse indirect illumination; then restore the recorded value. The switch controls screen tracing in screen-probe gathering, not every reflection or shadow feature. The source describes the screen-trace-to-fallback ordering. A change can reveal that screen-visible geometry was supplying information that the fallback representation handles differently. It does not, by itself, prove which fallback product is wrong; it tells you which representation boundary to investigate next.

16Change one room and follow the representations that must respond

Move the matte block while keeping its mesh and material. The capture script changes its mobility to movable and translates it by (−100,−80,0) cm. Its center moves from (77.5,285,52.5) to (−22.5,205,52.5). There is still one shared cube asset and the same material binding. Placement, bounds, visibility, shadows, tracing instances and affected lighting history must respond. This is why “the mesh changed” is an insufficient update message.

Now change only the light's intensity and color, leaving the moved block in place. The light becomes 7,200 lumens with linear RGB (1,0.55,0.25). The cube geometry and material base colors remain unchanged. Direct lighting changes immediately when the new light data is consumed; indirect illumination and histories need their own update policies. A material recapture is not inherently required merely because a light changed. Cached illumination is the affected quantity.

Return to the original room's tracing and caching views. Lumen's mesh distance fields describe geometric proximity for software tracing. Its cards parameterize surfaces for material and lighting storage. These two views answer different questions about the same seven components. A card is not a triangle acceleration structure. A distance field is not a material texture. A valid component transform must place both consistently, but their resolution, update mechanism, and failure modes differ.

The baseline and its extensions now connect the full architecture. Authoring objects provide semantic identity and editable values. Proxies and scene info organize renderer-owned behavior and membership. GPU records provide compact placement and material access. View passes resolve surfaces. Deferred shading consumes their properties. Lumen maintains additional geometry and radiance representations so light can arrive from surfaces beyond the camera's first hit. The independent Lumen walkthrough follows those caches numerically and visually; the present lesson is that a scene architecture must let each consumer maintain its own representation without losing track of which object and revision it describes.

The reproducibility bundle contains the room creation script, a small project-local editor bridge for verified viewport modes, engine configuration, exported scene inventory, capture commands, and image hashes. Internal proxy addresses, primitive packed indices and draw counts were not instrumented in this experiment, so the essay does not infer them from actor labels. For a future Arda implementation, expose these identities explicitly with generations and revision numbers. That would allow a trace to follow this very block from authoring edit to upload, draw, tracing update and lighting invalidation without relying on a screenshot to guess the transition.

17Deriving an Arda scene from the room

We can now design Arda's future scene layer from concrete obligations. The following is a proposal, not a description of existing Arda classes or a promise to reproduce Unreal's internal architecture verbatim. The room requires shared geometry, individually addressable placements, explicit appearance bindings, safe publication across execution boundaries, efficient GPU data, and several consumers of the same world. It also requires some consumers to use different representations. Those requirements are more durable than the exact names or allocation strategies of a particular engine version.

Begin with durable asset records. A geometry asset owns or refers to source geometry and its derived products. The conventional triangle product might contain vertex streams, indices, section-to-material-slot mapping, LODs, and local bounds. A future virtualized product might contain cluster pages and hierarchy data. A ray product might contain acceleration-structure inputs and build state. A volume product would have a different schema. These products should identify their source revision so a rebuild can be recognized and published without silently mixing new indices with old vertices. Asset identity should survive replacement of its current GPU allocation.

Next define a placed-object record. It references a geometry asset and material bindings, carries current and previous transforms, publishes conservative bounds, and identifies optional deformation or per-instance data. Use a handle with an index and generation at the public scene boundary. Internally, the renderer can map that handle to dense arrays and GPU allocations. The mapping is a renderer responsibility. Gameplay should never need to know whether a placement currently occupies GPU entry 400, because relocation and compaction must remain available optimizations.

A material binding should reference a compiled program plus the resources and parameters it needs. A geometry section selects a binding through a defined slot or index. Per-instance variation should have an explicit format, so the shader can distinguish a transform, an object-level tint, and a particle attribute. The compiled material describes relevant capabilities: opaque or masked coverage, displacement requirements, supported shading representation, and the domains in which it can run. This permits the renderer to reject an unsupported combination with a useful explanation rather than produce an accidental partial result.

Publish changes through typed scene operations. A transform update carries the new transform, bounds, and history policy. A parameter update carries a binding revision. A geometry replacement identifies a new asset product. A removal retires the public handle and schedules reclamation for the appropriate consumers. Collecting these operations into a scene revision gives the renderer a coherent publication boundary. It also permits coalescing: if gameplay moves the door three times before publication, the renderer may need only the final state plus a correctly defined previous observation.

// Proposed semantic records; these are not existing Arda APIs.
SceneHandle door = { index: 42, generation: 7 };

TransformUpdate {
    object: door,
    current: doorToWorldAtFrame121,
    bounds: conservativeDoorBoundsAtFrame121,
    history: ContinuousMotion
}

RemoveObject { object: door }
// A later replacement may use {42, 8}; stale {42, 7} updates fail.

The rendering scene consumes those operations and owns its read-mostly representation. It tracks which GPU records need uploading, which cached commands need rebuilding, which ray structures need updates, and which lighting representations need invalidation. These should be separate dependency consequences, not one undifferentiated “dirty” flag. A transform can update instance data and a TLAS entry. A topology edit can rebuild geometry-related resources. A roughness parameter can invalidate appropriate material or surface-cache state without forcing a new index buffer. Explicit causes keep both correctness and cost visible.

Geometry extensions should supply capabilities through interfaces with narrow responsibilities. A raster provider describes draw or compute-raster inputs. A deformation provider declares input resources, output resources, bounds policy, and history behavior. A ray provider exposes supported geometry and update requirements. An indirect-lighting provider can supply a surface capture or another representation when appropriate. These need not become four virtual methods on every object. They can be registered product types and handlers keyed by geometry kind. The essential requirement is that the core scene can discover and schedule them without knowing every specialized implementation in advance.

The shared GPU scene schema should start with only data broadly required for addressing, transforms, bounds, and flags. Optional payload ranges can hold specialized values. Otherwise each new geometry type will enlarge every object's record, increasing bandwidth for consumers that do not need those fields. Version the CPU-to-shader packing contract and test it with known records. Use the already measured matte block as the test object: its asymmetric scale, known corners, distinctive material, and recorded translation reveal swapped indices and matrix conventions. Keep the room baseline unchanged as a reference while exercising one update at a time.

A point provider exposes the value of explicit capabilities

Test the proposed design with a deliberately incomplete new feature: a point-cloud provider for the scan of this room. Its records contain positions and colors. It can generate camera-facing point footprints for the main raster view, but it has no UV coordinates, no authored surface normals, and no ray-intersection product. A flat vertex-color material is compatible with that declared raster interface. Our textured ceramic material that requires UV0 and a tangent-space normal map is not. Arda should reject that binding with the missing attributes named, or require an explicitly selected adapter that generates UVs and a documented normal convention. Silently feeding zeros would turn an interface mismatch into an unexplained visual artifact.

The same provider must report its ray capability as unavailable. A successful raster screenshot must not register an imaginary BLAS, promise an accurate mirror reflection, or imply complete GI participation. A later provider could generate triangles or finite ray-intersectable point geometry as a separate product, with explicit quality and update costs. A screen-space effect might still observe the visible footprints, but that observation disappears outside the image and is not equivalent to a persistent world-space tracing representation.

Now edit one scanned point. Its position update dirties the point buffer and conservative bounds, and it changes the raster representation that reads them. If a reconstructed triangle or ray product exists and depends on those samples, its source revision becomes stale and its owner schedules the appropriate update or rebuild. If no such product exists, there is nothing to pretend to update. Old in-flight draws keep the old buffer alive until their consumers finish; the newly published scene revision uses the replacement allocation. Changing only the point's display color can take a narrower path, provided no declared derived product uses that color. This is a small, testable extension of the scene's identity, dependency, and lifetime rules.

Keep persistent scene state distinct from frame work. The scene owns object identity, resource references, revisions, and temporal state. A frame builds views and schedules uploads, deformation, visibility, rasterization, lighting, and image processing through a graph of resource dependencies. Transient depth or GBuffer textures belong to that frame's rendering work; the tile asset does not disappear when those textures are recycled. Persistent lighting caches span frames but are owned by their subsystem and keyed to scene revisions. This separation gives a render graph useful freedom without making it the database of the world.

Streaming follows the same rule. A geometry asset can exist before its preferred LOD or cluster page is resident. The scene record remains valid while a resource manager selects a resident fallback or delays a particular consumer. Residency is not the same thing as object existence. Different consumers can require different products: a far object may need a coarse visible mesh, an occlusion representation, or a ray-tracing fallback. Making residency state explicit prevents one missing high-detail page from becoming a dangling scene reference.

Now run one proposed Arda frame of the extended room. Gameplay advances the door hinge and mannequin pose and changes the ceiling light intensity; enabling the optional effects fixture also spawns basin particles. It publishes a coherent batch of scene operations. The render scene resolves handles, updates world-space records and conservative bounds, and records affected representations. GPU uploads make changed primitive and instance data available. Deformation produces the character's current surface and the history needed for motion. View-dependent culling selects work for the camera and other consumers without destroying off-screen objects.

The raster path combines geometry access, material behavior, and pass requirements. Opaque and masked surfaces produce depth and the chosen deferred surface representation. Shadow work establishes relevant light visibility. Direct lighting evaluates the ceiling source against those surface properties. Indirect lighting queries the representations it supports, uses or refreshes persistent caches, and contributes reflected illumination. If their optional fixtures are enabled, transparent spray, mannequin hair, and mist follow their declared specialized paths and are composed into the image. Temporal and post-processing consumers use motion, history validity, depth, and color to produce the final display image.

At the end of that frame, several forms of the room still coexist. Gameplay retains actors and component relationships. The renderer retains registered objects and their render products. GPU buffers retain addressable scene records. Acceleration structures retain a form suited to rays. Lighting caches retain partial answers worth reusing. None is the universal master layout for every subsystem. They remain coherent because identity, publication, dependency, and lifetime have explicit contracts.

That is the essential structure of scene representation. A triangle became a shared asset; a placement gave it identity; a component made it authorable; a proxy made parallel rendering safe; GPU records made it efficiently addressable; pass processing made it usable by different raster operations; and additional representations made it visible to lighting queries beyond the camera. Arda can begin with a modest triangle renderer while preserving these boundaries. The value of the design is that adding a terrain patch, a simulated ribbon, or a new GI method then extends known contracts instead of forcing every system to agree on one increasingly overloaded kind of scene node.

18Extend the room until its geometry contract is explicit

We have followed seven cube components through the renderer. Now keep the same four-by-five-by-three-meter room, the same red and green walls, and the same matte and glossy blocks, and ask what changes when we furnish it. Three pots of repeated leaves introduce instancing. A mannequin introduces a skeleton. A cable, a breakable panel, smoke, and a basin each expose a different contract. The room stays our reference frame: every new object must explain what data it adds, who updates that data, and which rendering consumers can use it. This is the proposed Arda compatibility contract, not a claim that Arda already implements these adapters.

Separate the room's states before reading the diagrams. The baseline capture contains exactly five enclosing static-mesh surfaces and two static-mesh blocks, plus a separate rectangular light. The captured extension adds the mannequin, three pot instances, three stem instances, twenty-four leaf instances, and the hinged door with its indicator; the original seven placements stay fixed. The specialty fixtures below are explicit schematic alternatives or additions. A diagram of a cloth strip, groom, Landscape exhibit, Water body, or volume does not claim that the associated plugin is running in those captures. Nor do the alternatives all coexist in one crowded room.

The scope is the rendering families present in the inspected Unreal 5.8.1 source, including named optional plugins. Core adapter target identifies an early Arda implementation target; feature mode adds distinct evaluation or representation; plugin scope requires the corresponding plugin's assets and semantics. These planning labels are separate from whether a fixture appears in the captured room. A project claiming compatibility with content using one of these families must implement it or report the unsupported feature explicitly. Unreal permits additional plugins and custom components, so no finite built-in list guarantees arbitrary-project compatibility.

Each SVG uses the same room plan on the left and a magnified representation on the right. The yellow locator is an explanatory staging position; only the baseline component inventory and the captured extension report provide measured placements. The specialized diagrams are original schematics, not Unreal screenshots. Repeated instances, skinned surfaces, centerline-expanded ribbons, sampled points, and integrated density have different data contracts. FBX, Alembic, USD, LAS, or VDB names an import path, not the runtime primitive or renderer.
